passages.t: A house of prayer for all the nations
passages.happening:
‘This is what the LORD says’ (verse 1). They are to maintain justice and do what is right, because his salvation is coming soon (verse 1). The one who keeps the Sabbath and keeps his hand from evil will be glad (verse 2).

Then God speaks to two people who were afraid of being shut out. The foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD must not say that the LORD will exclude him. And the eunuch must not say that he is only a dry tree (verse 3).

To the eunuchs who keep his Sabbaths and hold fast to his covenant, God says he will give, in his house and within his walls, ‘a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters’ (verse 5). ‘I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off’ (verse 5).

The foreigners who join themselves to the LORD, love his name and keep his covenant, he will bring to his holy mountain and make joyful in his house of prayer (verses 6 and 7). Their offerings will be accepted on his altar, ‘for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’ (verse 7). The God who gathers the scattered of Israel will gather still others besides them (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 56 opens the last part of Isaiah, chapters 56 to 66. Its concern is the life of the restored community while it waits for God's salvation to be fully shown. The first question it takes up is who belongs.

Most scholars place these chapters after the first return from exile, when a small community in Judah was rebuilding the temple, finished about 516 or 515 BC, and arguing over its boundaries. Those who hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book read them as the prophet speaking to a community still to come.

The law of Deuteronomy 23 barred a castrated man from the assembly of the LORD and shut out certain foreign peoples. Eunuchs were common in royal courts, where men were castrated to serve as officials, often against their will. Isaiah had warned Hezekiah that some of his own descendants would serve as eunuchs in Babylon's palace. In a world where a man's name lived on through his sons, a eunuch was a dry tree with no future. God answers that fear exactly: a memorial and a name. The Hebrew words, yad vashem, are now the name of Israel's memorial to the victims of the Holocaust, founded in 1953.

Without a temple or land, the Sabbath was one of the few visible marks of belonging to Israel among the nations. It appears three times in this chapter as the sign of the covenant.
passages.later: Jesus quoted verse 7 when he drove the traders from the temple, saying that God's house is to be ‘a house of prayer for all the nations’ (Mark 11:17). In Acts 8 Philip meets an Ethiopian eunuch who ‘had gone to Jerusalem to worship’ (Acts 8:27), and baptizes him.
passages.hard:
Does Isaiah 56 contradict the law in Deuteronomy 23?

Deuteronomy 23:1 barred castrated men from the assembly of the LORD, and verses 3 to 8 shut out some foreign peoples. Isaiah 56 welcomes eunuchs and foreigners into God's house. Readers take this in different ways. Some see the prophet announcing a new stage in God's purposes, in which the old boundaries are opened, as the New Testament later describes. Others note that the law already made room for foreigners who joined Israel, and that Ruth the Moabite was an ancestor of David, so the prophet is drawing out an openness already there. Critical scholars often see a real debate within the community after the exile, carried in different texts.

On every reading the chapter's direction is plain. Faithfulness to God's covenant, not ancestry or the condition of a body, is what marks his people.
passages.asks: The eunuch called himself a dry tree, and God gave him a name better than sons and daughters. Ask what you have said about yourself that God has answered differently. And ask whom your church would quietly expect to stay at the edge, and what verse 7 says to that.

passages.happening:
The tone changes at once. ‘Come, all you beasts of the field; eat greedily, all you beasts of the forest’ (verse 9).

‘Israel’s watchmen are blind, they are all oblivious; they are all mute dogs, they cannot bark; they are dreamers lying around, loving to slumber’ (verse 10). Like ravenous dogs they are never satisfied. ‘They are shepherds with no discernment; they all turn to their own way, each one seeking his own gain’ (verse 11).

The chapter ends with the shepherds' own words, a drinking song. They call for wine and strong drink and say that tomorrow will be like today, only far better (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The watchmen and shepherds are the community's leaders, those meant to guard the people and warn them of danger. Watchdogs were kept to guard flocks and give warning. A dog that cannot bark is useless.

The call to the wild beasts is mocking. The flock is unguarded, so the beasts may as well come and eat. The leaders are asleep, or drunk, or busy with their own gain.

The chapter ends on the leaders' own words, which condemn them. They expect tomorrow to be like today, only better. Many scholars read these verses as the start of a unit that runs on into 57:13.

The chapter's two halves belong together. Outsiders who keep the covenant are welcomed in. Insiders who were meant to lead are exposed. From here to the end of Isaiah, the line between the faithful and the faithless runs through Israel itself, not between Israel and the nations.
passages.later: Ezekiel brings the same charge: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves!” (Ezekiel 34:2). Jeremiah had said the same of Judah's rulers: ‘Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture’ (Jeremiah 23:1).
passages.asks: The leaders expected tomorrow to be like today, only better. Ask whether that describes how you plan your own life. And ask, if you lead anyone, whether you are watching for them or for your own gain.
